summary: A Ness Labs article by Dr. Hannah Rose explaining the Zeigarnik effect and the Ovsiankina effect, two psychological phenomena in which unfinished tasks stay prominent in memory and create a pull toward completion. It describes how these effects can aid productivity, warns that long-unfinished tasks cause rumination and stress, and offers five practical steps for using unfinished tasks to advantage. Site navigation and newsletter boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: Explains the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects on unfinished tasks and gives five strategies to use them for productivity without harming mental health.
key_facts: Bluma Zeigarnik reported in 1927 that individuals tend to have a better memory for tasks that are interrupted or incomplete than for completed tasks.
The Zeigarnik effect was named after an observation by Zeigarnik and her supervisor, professor Kurt Lewin, about a restaurant waiter who remembered orders until each table left.
Zeigarnik explained that each task we start produces a form of psychological tension, which fades only once the task is completed.
Maria Ovsiankina, in 1928, found that individuals have a stronger urge to complete interrupted or unfinished assignments than tasks not yet started.
The Ovsiankina effect describes how not completing a task leads to intrusive thoughts and a strong desire to complete it.
Karen Horney described the 'Tyranny of the Shoulds', in which we compare the real self with the ideal self, and leaving tasks unfinished too long can impact self-esteem.
Oliver Weigelt and Christine Syrek discovered that leaving assignments unfinished over the weekend causes rumination and difficulty switching off from work.
The researchers found that spending a little time over the weekend finishing tasks or preparing for the following week could prevent rumination and stress, describing this as 'closure'.
Step one advises starting even if you cannot finish, since people feel more inclined to finish a started job at the earliest opportunity.
Step two recommends the ten minute rule to fight procrastination, noting people often keep going beyond ten minutes once started.
Step four suggests using the Eisenhower matrix or the MoSCoW method of prioritisation to delete or delegate tasks that remain unfinished too long.
Step five advises practising self-compassion and mindfulness through journaling, meditation, and exercise.
The article concludes that when not managed correctly, these phenomena can lead to cognitive dissonance and intrusive thoughts.
The Maker Mind newsletter promoted on the page has 80,000 subscribers and is described as a weekly newsletter with science-based insights.
